newsitem.title: SINGAPORE: Asia stocks end mixed, HK and Tokyo volatile.
newsitem.headline: Asia stocks end mixed, HK and Tokyo volatile.

text.p: Asian stock markets ended mixed on Friday as local factors dampened any enthusiasm for tracking Wall Street's spectacular overnight rally to its fifth straight record close.
Markets in Hong Kong and Tokyo were particularly volatile.

Partly propelled by the Dow's advance, the Hang Seng Index peaked at 14,145 early in the session only to drop to fday's low of 13,795 on futures-related selling. It finished up 188.21 points, or 1.35 percent, at 14,112.55.

"Market sentiment improved in the afternoon with mainland investors buying red chips," said Michael Ng, dealing director at Sassoon Securities. Red chips are Hong Kong-incorporated and listed companies with Chinese financial backing.
But analysts are uncertain if the market's latest correction is complete, noting the index has fallen about 907 points in five consecutive sessions.
"The rebound is not very strong considering yesterday's 497-point loss and the sharp gains in overseas markets," said Josephine Hui, head of research at Cheerful Research.
Tokyo stocks ended marginally lower after hitting a new high for the year early in the day. The Nikkei 225 index finished down 36.11 points, or 0.18 percent, at 20,528.35.
It hit a year's high of 20,791.08 early on, but the 181-point advance quickly eroded.
The rise had been supported by the settlement of June futures and options contracts, as well as a more stable dollar/yen rate and the advance in New York.
Traders said the settlement inflated midday turnover to a hefty 585 million shares from 190 million shares on Thursday. Once the settlement was over, trading eased.
"The market spent most of its energy on the settlement this morning," said Katsunichi Shimizu, general manager at Yamaichi Securities.
On Thursday U.S. economic data, mainly the third consecutive monthly decline in retail sales, suggested economic growth was slowing to a more sustainable pace.
The news sparked a rally in the U.S. government bond market, which in turn sparked a 136-point rally on Wall Street. At the close, the Dow Jones Industrial Average was up 1.79 percent at 7,711.47.
The slower growth scenario lent credence to the view that the Federal Reserve would not have to raise interest rates.
Figures on a key measure of inflation, the producer price index (PPI), and business inventories are due out later on Friday and could point the way for next week's direction.
The PPI is expected to show a rise of around 0.1 percent in May after a 0.6 percent drop in April, while inventories are forecast to rise 0.2 percent in April after a 0.3 percent advance in March.

Taiwan stocks rose, boosted by Wall Street's gains and renewed interest in the recently volatile electronics sector. The index ended up 55.74 points, or 0.67 percent, at 8,315.02, but below an intraday high of 8,355.87.
Korean stocks gained 14.49 points, or 1.87 percent, to close at 789.15, the highest such level since October 26, 1996, when it stood at 791.81.
The gains were led by buying of banks and blue chips.

Philippine shares closed 13.87 points, or 0.50 percent higher at 2,801.61, spurred on by the Dow's rise and news that U.S. brokerage, Merrill Lynch, had reduced its weighting on Hong Kong in favour of the Philippines and South Korea.
Indonesian stocks closed 3.4 points, or 0.49 percent, higher at 698.62, aided by an advance in property and banking stocks.

Singapore stocks ended virtually unchanged, making a partial recovery after earlier hitting a 28-month low of 1,978.31. The decline reflected bearish technical factors and disappointment over some recent earnings reports.
The Straights Times Index finished off 0.56 point, or 0.03 percent, at 1,990.12
The rally in New York failed to influence the markets in Thailand or Malaysia on Friday.

Thai stocks recouped some of the losses seen early in the session after concerns about liquidity problems among banks and finance companies. Nevertheless, the SET index ended off off 4.16 points, or 0.80 percent, at 515.60 -- a 97-month low.

Malaysian stocks fell sharply in reaction to April trade data which showed the country had posted a 2.1 billion ringgit trade deficit for April after March's 1.75 billion ringgit surplus. The market ended off 22.03 points, or 2.00 percent, at 1,078.38.

Australian stocks ended 17.2 points, or 0.65 percent, higher at 2,655.3, while New Zealand shares ended down 14.78 points at 2,366.29 led by a drop in shares of Telecom Corporation of New Zealand Ltd.
